newsitem.title: CONGO: Congo truce wobbles, U.N. seeks peacekeepers.
newsitem.headline: Congo truce wobbles, U.N. seeks peacekeepers.

text.p: Congo's ceasefire began to fray at the edges at the weekend, raising fears it might collapse before a mooted intervention force arrives.
Gunfire and occasional shells were heard overnight in the capital Brazzaville, where hundreds were killed in fighting before last week's truce.
The United Nations has begun the search for contributors to a mainly African peacekeeping force, either U.N.-approved or U.N.-led, of up to 1,800 soldiers at first.

The Security Council said such a force depended on a solid truce and proof that President Pascal Lissouba and rival Denis Sassou Nguesso wanted to find a political solution to the hostilities, which erupted as presidential elections neared.

"The ceasefire remains very fragile while there is no political solution and one seems far, far off at the moment," French ambassador Raymond Cesaire, the only foreign envoy left in Brazzaville, said by telephone.

France had 1,250 troops in Brazzaville to evacuate thousands of foreigners when the fighting started but pulled them out last week, ignoring a U.N. plea for them to stay until a peacekeeping force could arrive.

A similar African contingent in the neighbouring Central African Republic was caught up in fresh fighting by army mutineers at the weekend, an inauspicious sign for attempts to recruit a new force for Brazzaville.
Congo's warring sides have been left alone for now to find a solution, aided only by the local mediation of city mayor Bernard Kolelas.
He succeeded in getting rival military leaders to agree to extend the truce until next Saturday.

"The military are fed up, they don't want to fight any more, that's the feeling I got," Kolelas, whose own militia controls a neutral part of town, told state radio. "I have high hopes we'll do all we can to put an end to this drama."
Cesaire said a special session of parliament was due to be held on Monday to discuss the crisis.
The parliament building is in no-man's-land, where an international Red Cross team began for the first time at the weekend to pick up rotting corpses from the streets.
They had to dodge crossfire to do it and officials said a few people were still being killed or wounded during the truce, probably by "loose elements" at the end of unreliable lines of command.
There have been no face-to-face political talks between the supporters of Lissouba and the former Marxist Sassou Nguesso, whom he defeated in 1992 free elections.
The two rivals and Kolelas were front runners for elections due on July 27 which Washington, reportedly raising the threat of cutting off aid, has urged them to get back on track.
Sassou Nguesso says Lissouba's government is incapable of organising the poll fairly.
To go by the two rival radio stations broadcasting in Brazzaville, conciliation seems a long way off.
Sassou's radio said Lissouba's men fired on his "democratic and patriotic forces", looted the Italian embassy and was sending a trainload of arms up from the Atlantic coast to try to annihilate them.

Lissouba's radio said peacekeepers should come only to help oversee elections and not to freeze the city frontlines. "That kind of force would contribute simply to the Balkanisation of the Congo rather than to peace," it said.
